candidateRows: Robust non-naturalist realism best vindicates ordinary normative judgments and deliberation by treating objective normative truths as discovered, mind-independent, nonconventional, abstract facts.
This supplies the affirmative side's foundational route from ordinary normative phenomena to the existence and metaphysical character of objective normative truths.
David begins from judgments about reasons, wrongness, and truth-directed deliberation, then argues that adequately vindicating those phenomena leads to robust non-naturalist realism.
The fundamental realist dispute concerns normativity as a whole rather than morality alone, because moral truths form only one subset of normative truths.
The clarification fixes the proper scope of the motion-level disagreement and prevents the case from turning on a comparatively superficial moral versus nonmoral distinction.
David distinguishes moral, epistemic, and prudential normativity, identifies himself primarily as a normative realist, and treats divisions within normativity as less philosophically important.
A defense of realism must test whether it can answer epistemic, semantic, motivational, and disagreement objections while comparing its ability to preserve the phenomena with rival theories.
This establishes the affirmative's burden of proof and comparative method, specifying that initial fit with normative phenomena is provisional until objections and alternatives are assessed.

David acknowledges alternative dependence and error-theoretic views, then identifies knowledge, reference, motivation, and disagreement as objections realism must address alongside rival explanations.
Metaethical theories should be compared holistically by cumulative plausibility, and realism preserves much of what matters while imposing lower costs than competing packages.
The move provides the evaluative framework for the affirmative case and states its comparative conclusion without relying on an implausible claim of deductive knockout.
David rejects knockout expectations, proposes tallying plausibility across whole theoretical packages, and contends that realism delivers substantial benefits at a manageable theoretical price.

Historical and cultural variation in moral beliefs does not by itself undermine mind-independent moral facts, because facts must be distinguished from contingent beliefs and practices concerning them.
This blocks a major empirical route to anti-realism by separating variation in moral psychology and anthropology from the truth conditions of objective moral propositions.
David accepts that moralizing practices and beliefs have contingent evolutionary and cultural histories, while denying that this establishes any corresponding contingency in moral facts.
The central disagreement is between non-naturalist normative realism and global normative anti-realism, not between moral and nonmoral norms or necessarily between all realists and anti-realists.
This defines the negative side's actual thesis and narrows the debate to whether normativity as a whole has the objective non-naturalist status defended by David.
David's claim that normative realism is more fundamental than moral realism and that the moral distinction is comparatively superficial.
Lance accepts several framing points from David, notes affinities between naturalist realism and anti-realism, and locates their remaining dispute at the level of global normativity.
Realism has no automatic cumulative advantage when anti-realists reject alleged costs such as abandoning ordinary discourse or shared intuitions rather than merely accepting and outweighing them.
The move contests the affirmative's comparative methodology at its decisive input by denying that familiar realist advantages and anti-realist concessions should receive their assumed weights.
David's cumulative-plausibility claim that realism preserves more desirable commitments at a lower theoretical cost than rival packages.
Lance agrees that metaethics proceeds cumulatively rather than by knockout arguments but argues that opposing assessments of alleged costs can radically alter the package comparison.
Realist intuitions are neither universal nor an established default, and ordinary normative discourse and deliberation need not encode any substantive implicit metaethical commitment.
This attacks the proposed presumption for realism by disputing both the prevalence of realist starting intuitions and the inference from ordinary practice to realist commitments.
David's appeal to ordinary objective-seeming judgments and truth-directed deliberation as the phenomena that initially motivate and favor realism.
Lance reports lacking realist intuitions, emphasizes interpersonal variation, and argues that empirical study of language, behavior, and deliberation underdetermines both realism and anti-realism.

Existing disagreement-paradigm research poorly measures realism, and people's difficulty with such questions may reflect an absence of implicit metaethical views rather than defective measurement alone.

The methodological critique supports the negative side's conclusion that folk judgment supplies no privileged default for realism and that ordinary conduct can be explained without metaethical commitments.
The realist suggestion that ordinary disagreement, judgment, or intuitive responses reveal a default commitment to objective normative truth.

Lance argues that forced realist-versus-relativist classifications omit alternatives and mishandle cases, then proposes that ordinary people may possess no implicit view for such instruments to detect.

Empirical facts about what people think do not determine normative truth, and realism is the surface-level default because it directly explains objective normative facts rather than merely psychological activity.
This directly answers the negative opening by distinguishing truth from opinion and reframing the primary explanandum as normative reality itself rather than discourse, psychology, or behavior.
Lance's claim that empirical research into ordinary intuition, discourse, and deliberation removes realism's alleged default status and frames the relevant phenomena.

David denies that survey results motivate his realism, grants that folk metaethical views may be absent or incoherent, and argues that objective-seeming facts remain the central phenomena requiring explanation.
Moral inquiry must explain normative facts themselves, not merely the psychological fact that people hold normative beliefs.
The argument identifies the fundamental methodological divide: whether moral facts themselves or only psychological attitudes belong among the phenomena requiring explanation.
Bush's empirically oriented account of deliberation and ordinary moral judgment
Enoch accepts psychological deliberation as a legitimate explanandum but argues that wrongness itself is also initial data and that excluding it begs the question against realism.
Enoch's proposed normative explananda are not privileged because Bush lacks those intuitions and rival starting assumptions are equally vulnerable to question-begging.
The objection challenges the epistemic foundation of Enoch's realism by denying shared intuitions and demanding a non-question-begging basis for privileging them.
Enoch's claim that mind-independent wrongness is intuitive and must be explained
Bush denies the relevant realist intuitions, proposes that alleged apprehension of moral facts could be hallucinatory, and argues that further considerations are needed to adjudicate the dispute.
Failure to persuade someone who rejects a highly plausible starting point does not undermine its justification or place all starting points on an epistemic par.
This supplies Enoch's core epistemological defense of realist starting points and rejects the symmetry on which Bush's methodological objection depends.
Bush's claim that his contrary intuitions have equal standing with Enoch's realist intuitions
Enoch distinguishes different possible denials of wrongness, compares an unpersuaded opponent to a radical skeptic, and maintains that confidence in basic normative judgments can remain justified.
Enoch has supplied no argument for privileging his intuitions, and invoking how many people share them would reintroduce the empirical evidence Enoch discounts.
The move presses the unresolved burden on realism while exposing a potential tension between appealing to widespread plausibility and dismissing empirical inquiry.
Enoch's denial that realist and anti-realist starting points are epistemically symmetrical
Bush argues that Enoch has not justified treating realist phenomena as inquiry's proper starting point and says any population-based defense would require causal and empirical investigation.
Inquiry necessarily begins from what seems most plausible, and inability to argue an opponent out of rejecting such starting points does not threaten the position.
It states the positive epistemic methodology supporting Enoch's realism: basic normative appearances may legitimately ground inquiry without antecedent argumentative proof.
Bush's demand for a prior argument establishing which phenomena deserve explanation
Enoch says arguments cannot establish every starting point, invites comparison of normative wrongness with a merely psychological account, and treats the former as much more plausible.
If starting points require no supporting reasons, Bush is as dialectically entitled to begin from anti-realism as Enoch is to begin from realism.
The move crystallizes Bush's symmetry challenge by arguing that unsupported initial plausibility cannot confer dialectical priority on the realist position.
Enoch's claim that inquiry may begin with realist normative appearances as especially plausible
Bush accepts that each participant may start where things seem plausible but denies that Enoch has evidence, argument, or reason to prioritize the realist starting point.
The absence of further arguments does not make all starting points equally credible, and assuming otherwise commits Bush's methodology to radical skepticism.
This is Enoch's principal rebuttal to methodological symmetry, arguing that Bush's equality principle generalizes beyond metaethics into untenable skepticism.
Bush's claim that unsupported realist and anti-realist starting points must receive equal treatment
Enoch distinguishes superficial symmetry between any proposition and its negation from epistemic equality, then uses a radical skeptic to argue that Bush's principle is false.
Realists mistake normative opposition for metaethical evidence, while anti-realism can disambiguate counterfactual wrongness and empirically explain the resulting realist bias.
The extended argument offers an anti-realist explanation of ordinary moral language and realist intuition while claiming an evidential asymmetry favoring anti-realism.
Enoch's use of steadfast normative judgments as privileged evidence favoring moral realism

Bush interprets wrongness as expressing opposition, separates actual from counterfactual standards, cites sensitivity to normative and metaethical conflation, and proposes a selective debunking account.
Enoch's empirically detached reliance on introspection cannot establish methodological priority, so the debate may terminate in incommensurable starting points without adjudication.
The conclusion converts Bush's preceding debunking case into a general challenge to Enoch's method and denies that either starting point has established priority.
Enoch's accusation that Bush's psychological framing begs the question against realism
Bush argues that introspective philosophical methods remain open to empirical scrutiny, applies question-begging concerns symmetrically, and allows that no shared adjudicative principle may exist.
Inability to reach agreement does not imply truth or epistemic parity, realism uniquely accommodates normative judgments, and empirical data matters when it supports genuine debunking explanations.
The response integrates Enoch's epistemology, realism's claimed explanatory advantage, and a qualified role for empirical evidence in assessing moral intuitions.
Bush's claims of methodological parity, normative entanglement, and empirical debunking of realist intuitions

Enoch denies that failed dialogue establishes parity, says anti-realists cannot fully account for their normative commitments, and accepts empirical causal evidence when it genuinely undermines an intuition.
Realist arguments improperly rely on disputed assumptions, whereas ordinary moral improvement can be understood without those assumptions.
The move identifies question-begging assumptions as Bush's principal objection and invokes moral improvement as a phenomenon his anti-realist account must preserve.
Enoch's claim that Bush's presentation relies on a misleading tone of obviousness rather than a decisive argument.
After discussion of popular intuitions and empirical evidence, Bush redirects attention to whether realism can argue without presupposing its disputed conclusion.
Subjectivist paraphrases fit ordinary moral language poorly, and Bush's effort to accommodate counterfactual moral claims concedes the realist starting point.
This move connects linguistic evidence and counterfactual moral judgment to realism while arguing that anti-realist accommodation already accepts the central explanatory task.
Bush's attempt to explain moral improvement and counterfactual moral judgment without realist commitments.

Enoch answers Bush by arguing both that attitude-based paraphrases are linguistically inadequate and that accommodating stance-independent-seeming judgments places both sides in the same explanatory contest.
Ordinary moral language can support subjectivist analysis at least as well as realism, and realism is not needed to explain the relevant practices.
The move directly contests realism's alleged linguistic advantage and supplies Bush's alternative diagnosis that non-naturalist realism is a socially localized academic error.
Enoch's contention that subjectivist accounts distort ordinary language and implicitly concede a realist explanatory starting point.

Bush denies both parts of Enoch's challenge, arguing that anti-realist semantics perform equally well and shifting the explanatory burden toward why a small academic population adopts non-naturalist realism.
The scarcity of explicit realist belief among the general public does not count against realism, because most people lack developed views on similarly technical questions.
This is the principal realist response to Bush's sociological minority argument, separating lack of an opinion from disagreement and limiting the epistemic force of head counts.
Bush's claim that the tiny and socially concentrated population of non-naturalist realists is evidence against their view.

Enoch compares metaethics with interpretations of quantum theory, arguing that few people possess explicit theories and that numerical disagreement is at most secondary evidence rather than a substantive objection.
The epistemic challenge to realism concerns a shared causal history and unreliable philosophical methods, not a straightforward appeal to majority opinion.
The clarification supplies the mechanism needed for Bush's debunking argument: common training and methods may explain convergence without tracking objective moral truth.
Enoch's quantum-theory analogy and his objection that mere numerical minority status has no bearing on a philosophical theory.

Bush rejects the proposed analogy by contrasting empirically productive physical models with analytic-philosophical methods and emphasizes the causal origins of a small group's shared realist commitments.
A shared psychological error could causally explain realist belief even when most other people have no view, making raw numbers only a heuristic clue.
This move sharpens the debunking argument by specifying how a localized causal error could undermine realism without requiring widespread explicit anti-realist belief.
Enoch's charge that Bush must count everyone without an explicit metaethical view as evidence against realism.
Bush clarifies that the relevant consideration is an identifiable common cause of error, illustrated by a drug-induced hallucination, while treating population size merely as an initial indicator.
A demonstrated debunking explanation would matter, but numerical prevalence is not even a reliable heuristic because false views can spread widely.

The response concedes the force of a successful causal genealogy but blocks the inference from minority status, thereby narrowing the anti-realist challenge to independently supported debunking evidence.
Bush's claim that a small realist population can serve as a heuristic pointing toward a shared error-producing cause.
Enoch accepts that a proven causal explanation could undermine a belief but argues that either truth or error may become popular, so numerical patterns add no dependable evidential support.
Standard evolutionary and disagreement objections to realism are weak, but realism remains explanatorily superfluous and less parsimonious.
The move distinguishes Bush's anti-realism from conventional attacks and gives his core comparative case: moral phenomena require no realist posit and realism explains nothing better.
The moderator's request for additional anti-realist objections such as evolutionary debunking and peer disagreement arguments.
Bush declines to rely on familiar debunking or disagreement arguments, credits several realist responses, and instead locates realism's cost in explanatory redundancy and parsimony.
A pragmatist account can explain moral behavior, language, and psychology descriptively, dissolving realism by rejecting the shared framework of standard metaethics.
This is Bush's foundational positive case: realism answers no antecedent problem, while a metaphilosophical change of method dissolves the conventional realism-versus-anti-realism dispute.

Bush traces his method to pragmatism, ordinary-language philosophy, experimental philosophy, and cognitive science, then argues that descriptive explanation eliminates any need for realism or standard anti-realist substitutes.
Questions that appear intelligible have prima facie legitimacy, so quietism must provide arguments rather than dismissing difficult metaethical questions as misguided.
The move directly resists Bush's metaphilosophical strategy by shifting the burden onto quietism to explain why apparently coherent normative questions ultimately fail to make sense.
Bush's anti-realist quietist proposal that metaphilosophical inquiry dissolves the realism question rather than answering it.
Enoch answers the pragmatist framework with a presumption favoring intelligible questions and argues that merely denying a sufficiently difficult question is not philosophical progress.
His ordinary moral assertions report his own attitudes or dispositions in an appraiser-individual-relativist manner.
The move directly explains how the anti-realist understands his own ordinary moral judgments without invoking robustly objective moral facts.
The request to explain what his ordinary claim that gratuitous cruelty is wrong actually means.
After being asked how an anti-realist can sincerely condemn gratuitous cruelty, Bush characterizes his assertion as a claim about his personal attitudes or dispositions.
Moral assertions can combine propositional attitude reports with pragmatic expression of condemnation and readiness to oppose conduct.
This explains how anti-realist moral language can retain expressive and action-guiding force while still having propositional content about the speaker.
The request to explain the content and practical force of his sincere condemnation of gratuitous cruelty.
Bush supplements his attitude-report account with a pragmatic expressive component involving opposition, condemnation, and unfavorable responses toward the conduct and its agents.
His personal use of moral language does not commit him to a general semantic theory that moral sentences encode speaker-relative standards.
The distinction blocks an inference from his first-person anti-realist practice to a universal semantic analysis that he regards as linguistically inadequate.
The apparent inference that his account of what he means supplies the general semantics of moral sentences.
Bush denies being a semantic subjectivist because he is not claiming that moral sentences generally mean inconsistency with the standards of whoever speaks them.
Words and sentences lack context-independent meanings; people use them in concrete settings to convey communicative intentions.
The meaning-as-use account underwrites his refusal to turn a description of his own moral utterances into a context-independent semantic analysis.
The objection that his explanation of his own moral assertion sounded like an analysis of what such assertions mean.
In response to the semantic challenge, Bush rejects abstract sentence meanings and treats typical usage as an empirical matter concerning speakers' communicative intentions.
Communicative meaning may partly depend on communal practices, while speakers can lack complete introspective access to what they are doing.
The qualification addresses social and psychological complications that might otherwise undermine a purely individual-intention account of linguistic meaning.
The concern that his personal account must either determine sentence meaning or ignore broader linguistic practice.
Bush allows institutional or aggregated linguistic facts and concedes that his philosophical self-interpretation may diverge from how his behavior functions outside that setting.
Words and sentences do have meanings, even if those meanings may depend in some way on what language users mean.
The move challenges the anti-realist's meaning-as-use framework at the linguistic level, though David limits its force by disclaiming expertise.
Bush's claim that words and sentences themselves lack meanings apart from concrete acts of use.
Enoch expresses qualified suspicion toward Bush's philosophy of language and maintains that linguistic items bear meaning, possibly derivatively from speakers and social practices.
